rule_sets.py:480-486 float_literal_text returns f"{value:.16e}": one digit before the point plus 16 after gives 17 significant digits in exponent form (0.5 -> 5.0000000000000000e-01, -1e-05 -> -1.0000000000000000e-05, 1e-100, 1e+70, 5e-324 -> 4.9406564584124654e-324). 17 significant digits is the known sufficient count to round-trip any IEEE double, subnormals included, given a correctly rounded parser (MySQL uses dtoa-based strtod; not run here). _choose_prefix (src/sqllens/safety/rule_sets.py:365-376) collects lowercased names of every exp.Identifier in the tree, plus every key of `tables` and every name in each rule's `tables` (CompiledRule.tables = frozenset of tables the rule reads, rule_sets.py:561). It increments the index until no name starts with `sl<index>_`, so the chosen prefix is not a prefix of any collected name, case-insensitively. Hint inputs traced: (1) string-literal aliases: sqlglot parser _parse_alias falls to _parse_id_var / _parse_string_as_identifier, which build exp.Identifier (parser.py:9191-9230 in the sqlglot source found in scratchpad; a STRING token becomes an Identifier with quoted=True), so they are in the set. Var nodes are keywords or other non-name syntax, not table or alias names. (2) Column names listed in tables but absent from the statement: only the table keys are added, not the columns. Columns cannot collide with the guard's aliases or CTE names, which are table-level names, and the claim covers only tables, so this does not break it.
